name: The Newman-Tamburino Metrics
description: The vacuum fields whose light rays spread apart and shear without twisting, every one of which Ezra Newman and Louis Tamburino found in 1962. They come in two classes, a spherical one that changes with the retarded time and a cylindrical one, and both are algebraically general.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. Both charts are null charts built on the rays, $\partial_r$ along each ray with $r$ its affine parameter, and $u$ a retarded time labelling the null hypersurfaces the rays lie in.
history: Light leaving a source in empty space travels along null geodesics, and a thin bundle of those rays can do three things as it goes: spread apart, twist about its centre, and shear, stretching a round cross section into an ellipse. The vacuum fields whose rays spread with no twist and no shear belong to Ivor Robinson and Andrzej Trautman, who announced them in 1960 and solved Einstein's equations for the whole class in 1962 [robinson1960, robinson1962]. Rays with no twist are orthogonal to a family of null hypersurfaces, the wave fronts, which carry a retarded time $u$, while $r$ measures the affine distance along each ray [robinson1962, steele2004]. Which vacuum fields are left when the rays are allowed to shear?¶The answer came from the University of Pittsburgh in 1962, where Ezra T. Newman and Louis A. Tamburino kept the rays geodesic, expanding and free of twist, let them shear, and found every vacuum metric of that kind in closed form, unique up to a few arbitrary constants [newman1962tamburino]. Their tool was the spin coefficient method of Newman and Roger Penrose, Einstein's vacuum equations written out along a null tetrad, which they integrated directly [newman1962tamburino, newman1962]. They walked through the integration step by step on Robinson and Trautman's solutions, the members of the family whose rays do not shear [newman1962tamburino].¶The metrics split into two classes, which Newman and Tamburino called spherical and cylindrical [newman1962tamburino, degroote2008spherical]. Write $\rho$ for the expansion of the rays and $\sigma$ for their complex shear: the spherical class has $\rho^2 \neq \sigma\bar\sigma$, and the cylindrical class has $\rho^2 = \sigma\bar\sigma$, the rays spreading exactly as fast as they shear [degroote2008spherical]. In the spherical class the whole metric hangs on one length, $A = A_0 + b\,cu$, linear in the retarded time, through $a = A\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ on the wave front [steele2004]. Each ray comes out of $r = |a|$, where the Kretschmann scalar diverges, and from there the rays fan out and shear. In both classes the Weyl tensor has $\Psi_0 = 0$ along the rays, so they are one of its principal null directions [degroote2008spherical]. The field is of Petrov type I, with four distinct principal null directions, the rays among them.¶Which symmetries do these spacetimes have? The motions of the vacuum fields with hypersurface orthogonal, expanding geodesic rays were worked out by C. D. Collinson and D. C. French in 1967 [collinson1967]. For the spherical class they found a Killing vector only when $A$ is constant, $\partial_u$, a claim John D. Steele corrected in 2004 [steele2004]. Every spherical metric has a Killing vector: when $b \neq 0$, a shift of $u$ sets $A_0 = 0$, and the flow of $-u\,\partial_u + r\,\partial_r + 2x\,\partial_x + 2y\,\partial_y$ shrinks $u$ by the factor by which it stretches $r$ [steele2004]. Every one has a homothety too, $r\,\partial_r + x\,\partial_x + y\,\partial_y$, a flow that scales the whole metric by a constant whatever $A$ is [steele2004].¶The cylindrical class has a corner with more symmetry: in the limit Steele works with, $\partial_u$ and $\partial_y$ are both Killing vectors, and $2r\,\partial_r - x\,\partial_x + 2y\,\partial_y$ is a homothety [steele2004]. Its constant $\ell$ only sets the unit of $r$ inside a logarithm, and rescaling $u$, $r$, $x$, and $y$ together changes it to any value. The general cylindrical metric has a single Killing vector, and this limit has two [degroote2008cylindrical]. Its Kretschmann scalar, $16\left(3 - \ln(r^2x^4/\ell^2)\right)/(r^4x^4)$, diverges on $r = 0$ and on $x = 0$, and changes sign across the surface $r\,x^2 = e^{3/2}\ell$.¶An electromagnetic field whose own principal direction is the rays leaves only one class standing. Liselotte De Groote and Norbert Van den Bergh proved in 2008 that the spherical class has no such charged version, and integrated the charged cylindrical class completely [degroote2008spherical, degroote2008cylindrical]. With the charge switched off their solution reduces to the limit with two Killing vectors, and the general cylindrical metric, with its one, is left out [degroote2008cylindrical]. Twisting rays meet the same fate: for a vacuum whose geodesic rays expand, twist and shear, T. W. J. Unti and R. J. Torrence found in 1966 that the cylindrical type is the only one [unti1966]. The cylindrical class turned up again in 2013, as a special case of Jeandrew Brink, Aaron Zimmerman and Tanja Hinderer's reduction of axisymmetric vacuum spacetimes to three dimensions [brink2013].

related.text: The same untwisted, spreading rays with the shear switched off, every such vacuum found by Robinson and Trautman [robinson1962].
Newman and Tamburino's next vacuum, found with Theodore Unti a year later [nut1963].

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates of Ezra Newman and Louis Tamburino as John Steele writes them, $(u, r, x, y)$, with the retarded time $u$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ an affine length along the rays, and $x$ and $y$ pure numbers on each wave front, $\zeta = x + iy$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$ and flip Steele's signature. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Cylindrical limit

parameters.description: A length that sets the unit of $r$ inside the logarithm; rescaling $u$, $r$, $x$ and $y$ together changes it, so every value of $\ell$ is the same spacetime

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates John Steele writes for the limit of the cylindrical class, $(u, r, x, y)$, with the retarded time $u$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ an affine length along the rays, $x$ a pure number and $y$ a length. We write his constant $b$ as $b = -\ln\ell^2$, take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$ and flip his signature. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.
